capabilities.target: ERP vendor master including bank details

inputs.source: Supplier invoices uploaded to the supplier portal

instructions.note: Safety for payment and bank change relies on requesting approval, but the prompt does not require raw action details or independent destination verification.

controls.name: Clerk approval card before payment or bank change
controls.decay_rationale: The approver sees only the model's one line summary, not the raw action details. A more capable model can frame or omit critical details more persuasively, and the gate is also weakened by high approval volume.

controls.name: Raw action approval with bank account and change details shown
controls.decay_rationale: Would require the clerk to review the actual destination account, change history, and payment arguments from the system of record rather than a model summary.

controls.name: Recipient and bank destination confirmation bound to vendor master and approved record
controls.decay_rationale: Would bind payment destination and vendor bank change to the system of record so the model cannot substitute an attacker chosen account in the approval flow.

controls.name: Scoped ERP credential limited by vendor or action scope
controls.decay_rationale: Would prevent organization-wide vendor updates and payment scheduling beyond the approved scope.

controls.name: Detect and review anomalous bank changes and payment destination changes
controls.decay_rationale: An attacker can keep changes within normal patterns, so anomaly detection is detective and can be bypassed by stronger model behavior.

findings.title: Summary gated irreversible payment (TC9): untrusted supplier invoice can drive bank change and payment through a model-summary approval gate

attack_path.note: Supplier-controlled invoice content can assert new bank details and payment context.
Agent reads confidential vendor master data including bank details.
Agent can update any vendor bank details with broad ERP credentials.
Agent can schedule irreversible payment using the same broad ERP authority.

forecast.watch_signal: Model id or version changes in platform config without separate review, or approval is reduced/removed from payment and bank-change actions.

evidence.observation: The agent processes supplier invoices, updates vendor bank details when the invoice shows new details, and schedules payment.
The clerk sees only a one line model-generated summary for approval.
The card omits bank account numbers and change history, so the approver cannot review the raw action.
The clerk approves roughly 150 cards per day, which is high approval volume and raises fatigue risk.
The ERP credential can update any vendor and schedule any payment, making the agent a confused deputy with broad authority.
The model is upgraded with the platform and no separate review, so the summary gate is exposed to model_upgrade decay.

recommendations.action: Replace the one-line summary card with raw action approval that shows the actual bank account, change history, vendor identity, and payment arguments from the ERP record.
Bind payment destination and bank-change approval to system-of-record recipient data so the model cannot substitute an attacker-chosen destination in the approval flow.
Reduce ERP credential scope so the agent cannot update any vendor or schedule any payment outside a narrowly approved business scope.
Add targeted review of payment destination changes and anomalous vendor bank updates to detect abuse that passes summary approval.

stride_coverage.rationale: No protocol peer, agent card, or external identity assertion is described for this standalone agent design.
The artifacts describe no self-configuration, tool-definition changes, or mutable runtime configuration exposed to the agent.
No external data egress capability is described; the consequential harm here is payment and bank change, not disclosure.
The design does not describe open-ended loops, recursive delegation, or spend-amplification beyond individual invoice handling.
The artifacts do not say how supplier identity is authenticated at upload, so impersonation resistance cannot be assessed.
The artifacts do not say whether supplier uploads are attributable to a verified supplier identity with durable records.
This inbound cross-boundary flow brings supplier content in; the described risk is manipulation of actions, not disclosure on ingress.
No queue saturation, oversized file handling, or service exhaustion behavior is described for the invoice ingress path.
The outbound flow schedules payment in ERP; it is not described as a confidentiality breach across a trust boundary.
The design describes single payment scheduling decisions, not throughput collapse or resource exhaustion on this boundary flow.
The risk on this cross-boundary flow is unauthorized modification of vendor banking data, not secrecy loss in transit.
No evidence shows this bank-change path can be used to exhaust service capacity rather than alter payment destinations.
The artifacts do not say whether approval records are immutable or tamper-evident once the clerk acts on the card.
The approval record is described only as a clerk-facing approval artifact; no confidentiality exposure of the store is evidenced.
No dependency on record-store availability is described that would create a distinct denial-of-service risk in this design.

rating.rationale: Present risk is dominated by an untrusted supplier-controlled invoice reaching broad ERP bank-update and payment-scheduling capabilities. The only declared preventive control is a high-volume human approval gate that shows a model summary rather than the raw action, so rubric step 2 reduces critical to high but cannot reduce below moderate and does not sever the path. Forecast returns to critical if the model-summary gate further decays under model upgrade or is weakened/removed by autonomy changes. Manual validation applied because script execution was unavailable.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration artifacts provided, not observed runtime behavior.
No ERP tool schema, identity architecture, or audit logging design was provided, so the exact runtime data flow and record integrity could not be verified.
No source code or runtime enforcement evidence was provided for the approval gate, so its implementation is assessed as declared rather than verified.
